**The text.** This is the complete Text Artifact, exactly as it now stands:

````markdown
---
kntnt:
  genre: opinion
  technique: none
  language: en_GB
---

# Don't switch off Lervik's phone booking before we know what it costs

On 18 June the council executive board is asked to remove phone booking from all seven community venues from September. The officers' report gives one reason: staff should not have to enter the details in two flows. That is a fair thing to want. It is not yet a reason to make the change permanent.

## What the pilot actually counted

The pilot report *Bokning av föreningslokaler*, dated 8 April 2026, covers an eight-week trial in two venues. It records 96 bookings made on the web and 24 made by phone. Those figures are the report's, and so are their limits: it counts bookings rather than unique people, and it measures nothing about age, functional ability or how used to digital services people are. Twenty-four phone bookings therefore cannot tell us what share of Lervik's residents are unable to book digitally. Nobody should claim they can.

## A motive on the table, but no figures under it

The administration's objection to keeping both routes is double administration, and I take it at face value: it is not a claim that people who ring are lazy or expensive. But the documents contain no measurement of how long either route takes staff, and no calculation of what removing one would save. The board is being asked to close a channel for good on the strength of an inconvenience the documents put no number on. That is thin ground for making the change permanent.

## Six months, both routes, and something to measure

Öppna beslut proposes a six-month trial in all seven venues with both booking routes kept open. During it, the administration records the time each booking route takes and asks users to say, voluntarily, why they chose the phone or the web. We make no claim to have funded or costed that trial. What it would cost is for the board to weigh.

A booking made by phone is not proof that somebody cannot use the web. It is a reason to find out why the phone is still being used. I am not against digital booking. I am against settling its shape before the council can set the work each route costs staff against what it is worth to the people who use it.

## What the board can decide on 18 June

Postpone the permanent switch and run the six months with both routes open. When the trial has produced figures, decide whether a channel should be removed, changed or kept. That decision is the board's either way, and it will be a better one for being taken with the cost of both routes on the table.

— Sanna Ek, spokesperson for Öppna beslut
````

The officers' report gives one reason: staff should not have to enter the details in two flows. That is a fair thing to want. It is not yet a reason to make the change permanent." The anatomy requires both a standfirst and a lead, each working without the other. The measuring script takes this paragraph as the standfirst and reports the lead absent; whichever of the two the paragraph is taken for, the other is absent. What the reader loses: either a standfirst that can be shown apart from the body, or a lead — read with this paragraph covered, the body never states what the board is being asked to decide (removing phone booking from all seven community venues from September) before section 2 speaks of closing "a channel for good". Per the anatomy review guidance, an absent part is reported and not written: not from the text's own content and not from anywhere else. Leave this for a person to supply.

2. **Byline in the wrong place and form (article anatomy: Byline; opinion: identify the thesis holder early).** The text has a byline, but it stands as the last line — "— Sanna Ek, spokesperson for Öppna beslut" — where the anatomy places the byline after the standfirst, as one line in the English form `By <author>`; the measuring script therefore reports the byline absent. A part in the wrong place is present, not absent, and is repaired by moving it into place. What the reader loses: who holds the argument is not known until the final line, so "Öppna beslut proposes…" and "We make no claim to have funded or costed that trial" in the third section reach the reader before the text has said that Öppna beslut is the author's organisation and who "we" are. Preserve everything the findings do not concern: every sentence, every fact, every quotation, every code sample, every heading, every piece of formatting and every line of frontmatter among them comes back exactly as you received it — a repair that improves a paragraph nobody complained about is a change nobody asked for and nobody will review. A code sample — a fenced block, an indented block, or an inline code span — is quoted material rather than the text's own prose: its contents are read past rather than read against the rules, so nothing inside one is a finding and nothing inside one is changed, the docstrings, comments, and string literals among them. Prose about code is ordinary prose and is read like every other sentence. Where a finding can be repaired several ways, make the smallest change that removes it. Where a finding names something you cannot repair without inventing a fact, changing what the text claims, or altering a quotation's meaning, stance, certainty or distinctive wording, leave that passage alone and say so: in an ordinary review this text is answerable to material you do not have, and a plausible invention is worse than an unrepaired finding. For a brief-shortfall finding carrying exact source support, use only that support or the text to supply what is missing. Source Fidelity binds the repair: retain attribution, uncertainty, scope, chronology, causality and quotation meaning. A requirement in the brief is not source evidence; where the finding has no support for a needed fact, source or quotation, leave it for the writer and report why.

**A defect of your own costs the whole round.** The review that follows you establishes whether this text has a defect it did not have when you received it — a headline or a heading claiming more than the text claims, a heading repeating the passage under it, a limit your repair dropped. Where it establishes one, the whole round is rejected: the text you received is restored entire, nothing you did survives however much else you repaired, and no fresh attempt follows. So a finding you cannot repair without creating another one is a finding you leave and say so, exactly as you would one you cannot repair without inventing a fact — an unrepaired finding a person can settle costs less than a repair that has to be thrown away with everything beside it.

**What a repair may take with it, and what it may not.** A finding names a defect, and what a repair removes is that defect. Where the defect a finding names is the whole of the passage — an opening that would sit in front of any text, a closing that restates what the reader has just read, a claim credited to nobody that the text cannot source — removing it may be the repair, and any claim removed with it must be named in your return. That stops at a sentence whose work is to bound what the text asserts — that something is not measured, not claimed, not witnessed or not general, or that the text is an observation of a document rather than a scene from an occasion. Remove or weaken one only where the finding names a defect inside the sentence, and only where a sentence you keep still states that limit in full, so the text bounds what it claims exactly as far as it did, or where the limit contradicts another passage of the same text. Otherwise leave it exactly as it stands and say so. Where the passage carries a claim beside the defect — a fact, an observation, the point the passage exists to make — the smallest change is the one that leaves that claim standing, and deleting the passage entire is not that change. And where you can see no way to remove the defect that does not take the claim with it, leave the passage alone and say so, exactly as you would a finding you cannot repair without inventing a fact: a person can give that claim what it needs or let it go, and a round that deletes it leaves them nothing to weigh. That judgement is about the passage in front of you and never about how much of the text is left — a short text is no licence to leave a finding standing, and a long one is no licence to go on cutting.

A repair at a punctuation joint can be the smallest change even when the finding names the implication created there rather than punctuation itself. In *We finished in March, the finance team got a new reporting tool the same month.*, the defect is the implication created by joining unrelated claims, not either claim. Repair it as *We finished in March. The finance team got a new reporting tool the same month.*: splitting at the joint removes the implication and keeps the reporting-tool fact. Do the same wherever the named defect is confined to a joint; do not delete either side or supply a relationship the text does not establish. This example does not admit a wider mechanics pass: it identifies the smallest repair for the finding already in hand.

Before you return the text, compare it before and after, claim by claim. Every claim you received must still appear with its scope, certainty, attribution, chronology, causality and meaning intact unless the finding named the whole claim as the defect; that exception does not reach a sentence whose work is to bound what the text asserts, which goes only on the two conditions above, and the number or concentration of findings changes nothing about that check. The concentrated anti-slop case makes the boundary visible: removing its patterns must not discard its claims about meeting load, documentation, decisions, satisfaction, distributed work, adoption conditions, or the synchronous/asynchronous trade-off. Repair the patterns around those claims. If one cannot be separated from its pattern, keep it and report the finding unresolved; never compress several content-bearing passages into a cleaner summary.

Where the text is an `article`, a `casestudy`, a `column` or an `opinion`, measure it before you return it: run `uv run "/private/var/folders/cs/vgp_x_353zd9frkjpysp7zdw0000gn/T/kntnt-editorial-388-run-kb_ndw0j/home/.claude/skills/kntnt/library/scripts/article_anatomy.py" -` with the complete corrected text on stdin, under the same `UV_NO_CACHE=1 UV_NO_PROJECT=1` and fresh private `TMPDIR` terms as the resolver above. Exit 0 settles the counted requirements only: it says they hold and nothing about the anatomy requirements the script does not count, so your return reports the text as conforming to the anatomy only where you examined every one of those too, and otherwise names the ones you did not examine. Exit 1 names each counted requirement of the article anatomy that fails, with the part, the rule and the figure measured: repair the ones a finding named and the ones your own repair introduced, then measure again, except a part a finding names as absent and a failure caused only by an absent part, which you leave unwritten and name in your return as left for a person to supply; a requirement the text was already failing when it reached you, and that no finding names, is left exactly as it stands like everything else the findings do not concern. Exit 2 says the script could not measure the text, and your return says so. Read every `heading_pairs` entry against the complete candidate and the loaded headline contract before returning, whatever the exit status: judge whether each part adds different information in different wording. Necessary repeated names and topic words can be legitimate, and a paraphrased echo can share no words; `shared_words` alone never authorizes a change or creates a finding. Verify absent or ambiguous sentence estimates against the text; on exit 2 inspect the pairs by hand. Repair echoes named by the findings or introduced by your own correction by wording the heading from its whole text or section without strengthening its claims and without pre-spending the judgement, figure or concession of a quotation standing under a subheading, then measure again. An unrelated pre-existing echo stays as received and is reported in your return, with the pair and reader loss; the evidence does not expand your correction authority. Report any echo you cannot repair within that authority the same way.

**Your own working files.** Any file you write for your own working purposes — a candidate you measure, a draft you compare, anything you keep while you work — goes in a directory you created for this one round, under a name made unique when you created it, such as the one `mktemp -d` returns. Remove that directory before you return, including on failure. A fixed name under a shared temporary directory is not that directory, whether the directory is the system's own or a scratchpad your session was given: another run may be working at the same time, in the same place and on this same text, and write that same name. The file you come back to is then that run's work and not yours, and when you take it for your own stale copy and delete or replace it, you destroy work that is not yours, and nothing tells the run it came from.

**What you return.** The complete corrected text and a short note of which findings you repaired and which you left, with the reason for each you left. Where any repair removed a passage carrying a claim, name every removed claim and say which finding made the claim itself the defect, and name every changed claim the same way — one you left standing with its scope, certainty, attribution, chronology, causality or meaning moved, by what it now asserts rather than how far its wording moved, and the finding the repair that moved it answered. Where a repair took a limit, a connective or a bounding clause out of the text — a sentence or a heading saying what is not measured, not claimed or not known, a connective giving the text's own reason for what follows, a clause saying what a claim is not about — say what a reader of the text you return no longer has, however little of the text went with it. Name every added claim the same way, whether or not anything was removed: one the text you return asserts and the text you received has no counterpart for, an inference drawn from what that text already said among them where it asserts something that text did not say, and the finding the repair that wrote it answered. A claim with a counterpart in the text you received is changed rather than added. Reporting a removal never makes an impermissible one acceptable. The complete text: not a diff, not the changed passages, not a description of what you did. Return no commentary inside the text itself.

# Article anatomy

The fixed skeleton of a text in the genres `article`, `casestudy`, `column` and `opinion`; *article* below means a text in any of them. The anatomy fixes which parts the text has, their order and their dimensions. Angle, argument, voice and language are outside it.

A statement below has one of three strengths:

- A plain statement is a requirement: it holds in every conforming text.
- *Should* marks a norm: follow it as a requirement, and depart only when following it is impossible or the departure is clearly better for the reader.
- *Most* states what is typical across the whole text; each single paragraph or section follows its own content.

A text conforms when every part is present in the order shown and all three hold. Limits are exact; verify each one by counting.

A review of a finished text reports a part the text lacks as missing rather than writing it, and repairs only the parts the text has.

## Order

```text
Headline
Standfirst
Byline
Lead
Subheading        ┐ a section; one or more
Paragraphs        ┘
Last subheading   ┐ the ending
Paragraphs        ┘
```

Each part appears once, except the section, which repeats. The first subheading follows the lead directly. The body is everything from the lead through the ending.

The headline is the text's level-1 heading (HTML `h1`, Markdown `#`), and every subheading is a level-2 heading (HTML `h2`, Markdown `##`). The text should use these two levels only. Where an academic text would nest a level-3 heading, a further level-2 subheading usually serves; a level-3 heading is for the rare text whose structure truly demands one.

## Headline

- 20–70 characters, spaces included.
- It should be three to eight words and at most 60 characters.
- It is written as [Headlines](headlines.md) says.

## Standfirst

The standfirst is a summarising paragraph that introduces the article and stands on its own. It is a full paragraph; a deck — a subtitle or one-line teaser — is a different device and no substitute for it.

- One paragraph, at most 60 words.
- Self-contained: a reader who sees only the standfirst understands it fully.
- It says what the article is about and what the reader gains from reading it.
- It entices the reader to read on.

## Byline

One line naming the author. In English: `By <author>`. In another language, that language's conventional byline form. The author is the one the brief names; when it names none, the author is the user.

## Lead

The lead is the first paragraph of the body: one paragraph, meeting every requirement under *Paragraphs*. It introduces the subject and gives the reader a clear expectation of what they will learn by reading on.

### Standfirst and lead

Both open the text. Each works without the other, and read together they never repeat:

- The body reads complete without the standfirst, which is often shown apart from the body or skipped. The lead introduces every person, thing and event it mentions, and nothing in the body points back to the standfirst.
- They should begin with different first words, and an everyday word such as *the* or *it* counts like any other.
- Read in sequence, the lead advances. A reader who has just read the standfirst meets the lead as new material, never as the standfirst said again; what the body needs from the standfirst is named again in passing, and the lead moves on.

## Paragraphs

- Each paragraph holds one thought, and the thought sets its length. Most paragraphs come to two or three sentences. A thought that takes one sentence, or four or five, gets exactly that.
- A break may also fall for drama: a single sentence, or a single word, stands alone when isolating it creates an effect the text needs.
- Sentence length varies within the paragraph, giving the text a natural rhythm.
- A paragraph should be at most 80 words, so that a web reader takes it in at a glance. Eighty is the outer edge; aim well below it.

## Subheadings and sections

A section is a subheading plus the paragraphs under it.

- A subheading is at most 70 characters, spaces included.
- It describes clearly what the paragraphs under it are about, and it is written as [Headlines](headlines.md) says.
- A section holds at least one paragraph and should hold at most three. Most sections hold two or three.

## Ending

The ending is a section of its own, opened by its own subheading, after at least one other section. It is the last section, and it is short: one paragraph can be enough. It does two things:

- It shows that the expectation the lead set has been met.
- It calls the reader to action, and the action follows from the article's content. The selected genre says what that action is in its kind of text.

The last section is the ending when its subheading and paragraphs close the piece — the call to action, the reflection, the recommendation or the next step — and it opens no new line of argument. A section that carries the argument with a closing line appended is not an ending.
# Article anatomy — review guidance

Read under [the anatomy](article-anatomy.md), and word each finding in the strength the statement it rests on has.

A requirement that fails is a finding. Count characters and words before reporting a limit, and give the count.

A part the text does not have is reported, and a part it has is repaired. Where a required part is absent — the headline, the standfirst, the byline, the lead, a section, or the ending with its call to action — its absence is a finding, and the part is not written: not from the text's own content and not from anywhere else, since the text is finished and a person decides what fills it. A part the text has that fails its own rule is repaired like any other defect, from the text's own content. A part in the wrong place is present, not absent, and is repaired by moving it into place: a byline standing at the end of the text is moved to its place in the order, although the measuring script reports the byline `absent`. Ending content the text has — closing paragraphs that show the lead's expectation met or call the reader to act — is a present ending. Where the last section is an ending by the anatomy's test, a defect in it, a vague call to action among them, is repaired where it stands from what the text already says. Where the closing content stands inside a last section that carries the argument, or inside a text's only section, it is a present ending that fails its rule, since the ending is a section of its own: it is repaired by giving it a section of its own, opened by its own subheading and built from the text's own content, the closing content moving there and a vague call to action among it repaired from what the text already says. At the close of a text with no section at all, closing content is repaired where it stands from what the text already says, and no section and no subheading is written to hold it: the text has no ending section either, and that is reported with its absent sections. A text with no ending content at all has an absent ending, and a text that calls the reader to no action has an absent call to action; both are reported. A failure the script reports only because another part is absent is reported as that absent part and is not repaired by writing it: a lead of several paragraphs in a text with no subheading fails only because its sections are absent, so the finding is the absent sections, and no section and no subheading is written to make the lead one paragraph. Likewise a text of one section with no ending content fails the section count only because its ending is absent, and the finding is the absent ending. Where the script takes the text's one opening paragraph as its standfirst and reports the lead absent, whichever of the two that paragraph is taken for, the other is absent and is reported.

A departure from a *should* is a finding only when following the norm was possible and the text is no better for having left it. A paragraph a little past the edge that holds one thought and reads well at that length has met the bar. A paragraph far past it, or paragraphs that run long throughout, cost the web reader something a finding can name. The anatomy's bands are its four *should* norms on a dimension, each with the figure [the anatomy](article-anatomy.md) gives it: the headline's word norm and its character norm, a paragraph's word norm, and a section's paragraph norm. A band is not by itself a defect. A headline, a subheading or a paragraph the text has that meets its requirements is not rewritten, split or merged only to come inside a band. A change the test above justifies is not made only to come inside one: it repairs what the finding names the reader losing, as a split of a paragraph far past the edge does. The limits the script reports as failures are requirements, not bands — the headline's character limits, a subheading's maximum, and the standfirst's single paragraph and its word limit, each as the anatomy states it — and a part that fails one is repaired. A subheading has no band, only its maximum. A subheading that describes clearly what its section is about meets its requirement, and is not rewritten from a label into a statement on that ground alone; one that does not describe its section fails that requirement and is repaired.

*Most* is read across the whole text, and no single paragraph or section fails it. A four-sentence paragraph is no finding. A paragraph holding two thoughts is one, and so is a text whose paragraphs are nearly all a single sentence or nearly all long. Name the pattern and what it costs the reader rather than the count.

Read the standfirst separately, then with the lead. Can it introduce the piece on its own, and does the lead start doing the promised work? Repeated orientation may be necessary; an opening that restarts without advancing is the defect. Then read the body with the standfirst covered. A pronoun, a definite form or a phrase such as *the reason* whose referent only the standfirst supplies is a finding, repaired by naming the referent where the body first needs it.

In a text under review, the author is whoever the text, its metadata or the invocation names. A byline nobody can name is reported as missing and left unfilled: the reviewer's user is not presumed to have written a text they brought for review.

# Opinion

A journalistic debate article that argues a clear position and asks for a change or a considered stance. The author takes responsibility for the argument rather than observing it from outside.

Apply the shared [web craft brief](../web-craft.md).

Follow the [article anatomy](../article-anatomy.md).

Write the headline and the subheadings as [Headlines](../headlines.md) says.

## What this genre asks for

State the thesis early and identify its holder when an author is supplied. Let the headline and useful subheadings carry the issue and argument for a scanning reader.

Build a case the reader can follow, distinguishing evidence, judgement and inference. Attribute load-bearing factual claims where they are used, and meet relevant real objections fairly. Neither an argument quota nor an invented opponent makes the case stronger.

Keep a persuasive, accountable voice without strengthening or weakening the author's supplied positions: absence of opposition is not endorsement. Criticise ideas, decisions and actions precisely; do not invent an opponent's motives. Preserve warranted sharpness as well as material qualifications, without compulsory softening or inflated rhetoric.

The call to action is the specific change or stance the argument supports, and the ending makes clear who can act. Reconsidering or declining a proposal can be the action; a generic exhortation alone is not one.

## The technique this genre is ordinarily written with

None.
# Opinion — review guidance

Identify the early position, the grounds supporting it and the action the ending leaves with somebody. If *it is time to act* names no act, look for the existing proposal to make explicit; supply no new policy or decision.

Check factual premises and predictions against the support visible in the text, loaded figures for attribution, and objections for fair treatment. Treat a clearly proposed target with its stated uncertainty as an authorial choice. A support finding identifies a premise or inferential dependency the argument actually asserts; preserve choices that make no such factual promise. An internal contradiction or broken inference is a finding; external reference checking is outside this review.

Preserve a successful polemic, its authorial responsibility and its qualifications. A pointed closing or rhetorical return is not a defect because a neutral report would omit it. Clarify a broken argument without replacing its position.

# Don't switch off Lervik's phone booking before we know what it costs

On 18 June the council executive board is asked to remove phone booking from all seven community venues from September. The officers' report gives one reason: staff should not have to enter the details in two flows. That is a fair thing to want. It is not yet a reason to make the change permanent.

By Sanna Ek, spokesperson for Öppna beslut

## What the pilot actually counted

The pilot report *Bokning av föreningslokaler*, dated 8 April 2026, covers an eight-week trial in two venues. It records 96 bookings made on the web and 24 made by phone. Those figures are the report's, and so are their limits: it counts bookings rather than unique people, and it measures nothing about age, functional ability or how used to digital services people are. Twenty-four phone bookings therefore cannot tell us what share of Lervik's residents are unable to book digitally. Nobody should claim they can.

## A motive on the table, but no figures under it

The administration's objection to keeping both routes is double administration, and I take it at face value: it is not a claim that people who ring are lazy or expensive. But the documents contain no measurement of how long either route takes staff, and no calculation of what removing one would save. The board is being asked to close a channel for good on the strength of an inconvenience the documents put no number on. That is thin ground for making the change permanent.

## Six months, both routes, and something to measure

Öppna beslut proposes a six-month trial in all seven venues with both booking routes kept open. During it, the administration records the time each booking route takes and asks users to say, voluntarily, why they chose the phone or the web. We make no claim to have funded or costed that trial. What it would cost is for the board to weigh.

A booking made by phone is not proof that somebody cannot use the web. It is a reason to find out why the phone is still being used. I am not against digital booking. I am against settling its shape before the council can set the work each route costs staff against what it is worth to the people who use it.

## What the board can decide on 18 June

Postpone the permanent switch and run the six months with both routes open. When the trial has produced figures, decide whether a channel should be removed, changed or kept. That decision is the board's either way, and it will be a better one for being taken with the cost of both routes on the table.
EOF

The pilot report *Bokning av föreningslokaler*, dated 8 April 2026, covers an eight-week trial in two venues. It records 96 bookings made on the web and 24 made by phone. Those figures are the report's, and so are their limits: it counts bookings rather than unique people, and it measures nothing about age, functional ability or how used to digital services people are. Twenty-four phone bookings therefore cannot tell us what share of Lervik's residents are unable to book digitally. Nobody should claim they can.

## A motive on the table, but no figures under it

The administration's objection to keeping both routes is double administration, and I take it at face value: it is not a claim that people who ring are lazy or expensive. But the documents contain no measurement of how long either route takes staff, and no calculation of what removing one would save. The board is being asked to close a channel for good on the strength of an inconvenience the documents put no number on. That is thin ground for making the change permanent.

## Six months, both routes, and something to measure

Öppna beslut proposes a six-month trial in all seven venues with both booking routes kept open. During it, the administration records the time each booking route takes and asks users to say, voluntarily, why they chose the phone or the web. We make no claim to have funded or costed that trial. What it would cost is for the board to weigh.

A booking made by phone is not proof that somebody cannot use the web. It is a reason to find out why the phone is still being used. I am not against digital booking. I am against settling its shape before the council can set the work each route costs staff against what it is worth to the people who use it.

## What the board can decide on 18 June

Postpone the permanent switch and run the six months with both routes open. When the trial has produced figures, decide whether a channel should be removed, changed or kept. That decision is the board's either way, and it will be a better one for being taken with the cost of both routes on the table.
